lessons.title: What a SOC actually does
lessons.summary: A Security Operations Center continuously collects signals, separates noise from risk, coordinates response, and improves detection coverage. Analysts are evidence-driven, not alert-closing machines.
details: Monitoring means observing; detection means recognizing suspicious patterns; response means controlling an incident
A detection is a hypothesis, not proof of compromise
Every action should be traceable in a ticket with timestamps and supporting artifacts
workflow: Identify the business asset and owner
Understand alert source, rule logic and timeframe
Check evidence, determine impact and document the result
lessons.example: An impossible-travel alert alone is weak; correlate sign-ins, MFA method, device and IP before escalating.

lessons.title: L1 vs L2 vs L3 responsibilities
lessons.summary: L1 validates alerts and follows playbooks; L2 conducts scoping, deeper correlation and response; L3 handles complex investigations, threat hunting, detection engineering and mentoring. Exact job boundaries vary by organization.
details: L1: triage, enrichment, severity, escalation, shift notes
L2: timeline reconstruction, identity/endpoint pivoting, containment proposals, incident coordination
L3: hypothesis hunts, custom detection development, attack simulation, root-cause analysis
workflow: State the evidence and confidence level
Escalate based on impact, scope, privilege and policy
Hand off with what was checked, what was not and next actions
lessons.example: A likely stolen admin session is escalated to L2 immediately; L3 later creates a new detection for the observed token-abuse pattern.

lessons.title: A complete SOC shift
lessons.summary: A repeatable shift starts with handover, sensor health, backlog and intelligence review, then prioritizes alerts and maintains accurate case updates.
details: Critical outstanding incidents take priority over fresh low-fidelity alerts
Missing logs and dead sensors are security issues, not just IT tickets
SLA and escalation timers vary by company
workflow: Read prior shift handover and open incidents
Confirm key telemetry ingesting; inspect urgent queues
Work highest-risk alerts, communicate, and write the next handover
lessons.example: At shift start, the EDR connector stopped sending logs 40 minutes ago; open a collection-gap incident before declaring hosts quiet.

lessons.title: OSI, TCP/IP and encapsulation
lessons.summary: Traffic is packaged across link, IP, transport and application layers. Understanding where a signal belongs helps isolate malicious behavior from ordinary connectivity issues.
details: IP routes packets between networks; TCP or UDP distinguishes transport behavior
TCP sessions use flags, sequence and acknowledgement numbers
DNS and HTTP are application protocols carried by lower layers
workflow: Identify source, destination, protocol and ports
Decide which device or log can observe the behavior
Check whether capture covers both directions
lessons.example: A firewall sees TCP 443 but cannot infer the URL path without relevant TLS inspection or proxy logs.

lessons.title: IP addresses, CIDR and NAT
lessons.summary: IPv4 addresses identify interfaces; CIDR masks define network boundaries. NAT rewrites addresses and sometimes ports, so public IP alone may not identify an internal device.
details: RFC1918 private ranges are 10/8, 172.16/12 and 192.168/16
A /24 has 256 addresses, conventionally 254 usable hosts on a typical subnet
Source port plus translation logs may be necessary to attribute shared egress
workflow: Convert source and destination to private/public scope
Check subnet membership and routing
When NAT is involved, request timestamped translation records
lessons.example: An external service records 203.0.113.9; the NAT gateway maps its source port to workstation 10.10.8.24.

lessons.title: Ports and common services
lessons.summary: Ports identify transport endpoints; the protocol and application content determine the real service. Unusual ports can be normal and default ports can carry malicious traffic.
details: DNS 53 TCP/UDP, HTTP 80 TCP, HTTPS 443 TCP or UDP/QUIC
SSH 22, SMB 445, RDP 3389, LDAP 389, LDAPS 636
Kerberos 88, SMTP 25/587, NTP 123, DHCP 67/68
workflow: Verify protocol not just port number
Compare destination to allowed business services
Inspect DNS, proxy or application context
lessons.example: Outbound 445 to the internet from an office endpoint deserves investigation even if firewall prevented the connection.

lessons.title: TCP handshake, flags and resets
lessons.summary: TCP uses SYN → SYN/ACK → ACK to establish state. Flags, retransmits and RST packets help explain scanning, failed connections and disruption.
details: SYN without replies may indicate filtering, loss or unreachable hosts
Repeated SYNs to sequential ports may be scanning but can also be monitoring
A reset terminates a connection; context decides whether it is malicious
workflow: Build a chronological packet timeline
Compare number of destinations, ports and attempts
Validate with firewall and endpoint process information
lessons.example: A burst of SYN packets across 1,000 ports from one workstation after office hours suggests reconnaissance.

lessons.title: DNS from query to answer
lessons.summary: A resolver looks up records, caches responses based on TTL and can query authoritative servers. DNS logs expose destinations and sometimes command-and-control patterns.
details: A/AAAA map hosts to IPs; CNAME aliases; MX handles mail
NXDOMAIN means the name does not exist; repeated failures can suggest domain-generation activity
TXT, SRV and PTR records have legitimate uses and can be abused
workflow: Inspect query, response, timestamp and client
Measure volume, length, entropy and NXDOMAIN ratio
Correlate unusual domains with processes and network flows
lessons.example: A workstation queries dozens of random-looking subdomains every 10 seconds; compare against normal telemetry before labeling tunneling.

lessons.title: HTTP, HTTPS, headers and status codes
lessons.summary: Web requests include methods, paths, headers and bodies. TLS hides content from observers without decryption, but certificates, destination and metadata can still be useful.
details: 200 success; 301/302 redirect; 401 authentication required; 403 forbidden
404 not found; 429 rate limited; 500 server error
User-Agent and referrer can support investigation but are easily spoofed
workflow: Review method, URL path, status, user agent and response size
Look for patterns across requests rather than one suspicious string
Check identity and endpoint telemetry
lessons.example: A POST to /upload with a large body after suspicious login is worth reviewing against approved application behavior.

lessons.title: TLS and certificates
lessons.summary: TLS protects data in transit using authenticated key exchange and symmetric encryption. Certificate validation authenticates a claimed server identity but does not make a site trustworthy.
details: SNI may expose hostname unless encrypted client hello is in use
The certificate chain, validity and SAN matter during verification
A valid certificate is compatible with phishing, malware and command-and-control
workflow: Review client and server TLS metadata
Check certificate issuer, age, SAN and expected hostname
Correlate with DNS and proxy observations
lessons.example: A freshly registered host with a valid Let's Encrypt certificate is not automatically safe or malicious.

lessons.title: Linux essentials for analysts
lessons.summary: Processes, permissions, services and logs reveal system behavior. Knowing common directories and commands shortens response time.
details: /var/log contains many service logs, but locations depend on distro
sudo, su, cron, systemd and SSH leave useful traces
Processes, sockets and service configurations should be collected carefully
workflow: Inspect journalctl, auth logs and process tree
Check systemd timers, cron and active sockets
Preserve output with timestamps and case references
lessons.example: A new systemd service executes a binary in /tmp at startup; investigate provenance and owner.

lessons.title: Windows internals and event logs
lessons.summary: Windows generates security, system, application and other telemetry. Processes, services, tasks, registry keys and authentication all provide investigative pivots.
details: 4624 successful logon; 4625 failed logon; 4688 process creation when enabled
7045 often indicates a new service; 1102 indicates Security log cleared
Sysmon provides additional optional process, network and other event visibility
workflow: Check time synchronization and enabled audit policy
Correlate user, Logon ID, host and parent-child process
Search related hosts for similar activity
lessons.example: An encoded PowerShell process launched by a document application is suspicious when the user denies running scripts.

lessons.title: Identity, AD, LDAP and Kerberos
lessons.summary: In Active Directory, users, groups, computers and domain controllers govern access. Kerberos tickets and LDAP queries are normal operations that also appear in attacks.
details: A TGT enables a client to request service tickets; a TGS authorizes access to a service
Group membership and delegated privileges determine access boundaries
Kerberos failures have many causes; distinguish user typo from attack by volume and pattern
workflow: Understand source host, account, target and logon type
Check privileged group membership and recent changes
Pivot into DC security logs and sign-in activity
lessons.example: A service account suddenly requests tickets for many unfamiliar SPNs; investigate whether the application changed before claiming Kerberoasting.

lessons.title: Processes, hashes and digital signatures
lessons.summary: An executable's path, lineage, signer, hash, command line and prevalence give context. A file hash identifies exact bytes, not intent.
details: SHA-256 can correlate identical file content across hosts
A signed binary can be abused as a living-off-the-land tool
An unsigned binary is not necessarily malicious
workflow: Inspect process tree and full command line
Check signature, hash reputation and known-good baselines
Find the same hash or behavior across the environment
lessons.example: A signed rundll32.exe launched from an unusual parent with odd arguments may warrant more scrutiny than unsigned test software.

lessons.title: CIA, AAA and least privilege
lessons.summary: Confidentiality, integrity and availability describe security goals. Authentication proves a claim, authorization controls actions and accounting records activity.
details: MFA reduces password-only risk but does not stop all session theft
Least privilege limits blast radius from compromised identities
Service accounts need controlled credentials and scoped permissions
workflow: Identify which CIA property is at risk
Check account role and resource sensitivity
Recommend least-privilege remediation
lessons.example: A compromised read-only account is not equivalent in severity to compromised tenant-wide administrator access.

lessons.title: Threats, vulnerabilities, risk and IOCs
lessons.summary: A vulnerability is a weakness; an exploit abuses it; an IOC is an observable artifact; a TTP describes behavior. Risk combines likelihood, exposure and impact.
details: IP and hash indicators can be brittle; behavior often lasts longer
CVE identifiers catalog publicly disclosed vulnerabilities, not proof of compromise
Severity ratings like CVSS need environmental context
workflow: Separate technical observation from inference
Assess exploitability, exposure, business impact and compensating controls
Corroborate IOC hits with related activity
lessons.example: A critical CVE on an isolated test server may be less urgent than an exploited medium-rated flaw on an exposed authentication gateway.

lessons.title: MITRE ATT&CK and the kill chain
lessons.summary: ATT&CK organizes observed adversary tactics and techniques; a kill-chain model summarizes phases. Neither proves an incident by itself.
details: Tactics describe why adversaries act; techniques describe how
One command can map to multiple techniques depending on context
Defense coverage should consider prevention, visibility and detection
workflow: Identify suspicious behavior before picking a technique
Map it to supported ATT&CK technique IDs
List the telemetry needed to confirm the hypothesis
lessons.example: Credential dumping behavior maps to T1003; the supporting evidence is process, access and security product telemetry, not merely a label.

lessons.title: Telemetry quality and time normalization
lessons.summary: The SOC can only investigate what it can see. Ingest delay, parsing failure, clock drift and retention gaps distort incident reconstruction.
details: UTC timestamps avoid daylight-saving ambiguity
Source time, ingestion time and event time may differ
Missing fields can invalidate correlation logic
workflow: Check connector freshness and parsing coverage
Normalize times before comparing products
Flag blind spots and limits in conclusions
lessons.example: A VPN login seems to precede a phishing click until one log source is converted from local time to UTC.

lessons.title: The first five minutes of an alert
lessons.summary: Triage means deciding whether an alert is real, relevant and urgent enough for action. A fast, repeatable sequence improves consistency.
details: Alert rule logic and data source are part of the evidence
True positive does not always mean a confirmed security incident
Do not run destructive actions solely because a detection fired
workflow: Validate alert timestamps, affected entity and signal
Check asset criticality, identity privilege and historical baseline
Pivot to related telemetry and record next step
lessons.example: A malware label without an execution event is not the same as confirmed ransomware on a production file server.

lessons.title: True positive, false positive and benign positive
lessons.summary: A true positive correctly matches the detection; a benign positive is an expected but suspicious-pattern behavior; a false positive is inaccurate rule logic or parsing. Labels vary across SOC platforms.
details: A legitimate admin action may trigger an accurate detector
Incident disposition should record rationale, not just label
Don't suppress a noisy detection without understanding what it would miss
workflow: Reconstruct exactly what the rule matched
Determine whether observed activity was authorized and harmful
Document decision with business context and verification
lessons.example: A planned vulnerability scan triggers port-scan detection: accurate detection, authorized activity, typically benign positive.

lessons.title: Severity, priority and escalation
lessons.summary: Severity reflects impact/technical seriousness; priority reflects urgency relative to business context, SLA and competing cases. Frameworks differ by employer.
details: Production outages, privileged compromise and active spread increase urgency
Confidence is distinct from severity: high impact with low confidence still needs careful escalation
Actions must follow authorization and incident-handling playbooks
workflow: Evaluate asset criticality, user privilege, scope and activity status
Assign severity with a transparent justification
Escalate with artifact links, timeline and requested action
lessons.example: A compromised domain admin account gets priority even if initial evidence is incomplete, because the potential blast radius is large.

lessons.title: A high-quality ticket and handoff
lessons.summary: A useful ticket lets the next analyst continue without repeating work. Evidence, analytical judgment and uncertainty should be clearly separated.
details: Include who/what/where/when/how, detection and correlation ID
Record negative checks and limitations, not only positive hits
Preserve links or snapshots of volatile telemetry
workflow: Write a one-sentence summary and business impact
Add timeline, IOCs, evidence, hypotheses and confidence
Document containment performed or recommended and owner/next action
lessons.example: Case 1042: 09:12 UTC suspicious inbox rule; 09:20 correlated new sign-in from unusual ASN; session revocation requested, awaiting IAM approval.

lessons.title: Windows sign-in events
lessons.summary: Successful and failed authentication events must be interpreted with logon type, status, account and source. One failed login is usually ordinary.
details: 4624 includes logon types: 2 interactive, 3 network, 10 remote interactive
4625 has failure details and source metadata when present
4740 identifies account lockouts; 4768/4769/4771 support Kerberos analysis
workflow: Group by account and source over time
Compare failure bursts with success and geography/ASN
Verify service accounts and known scanners
lessons.example: Thirty 4625 failures followed by a 4624 from the same external jump host is more concerning than routine typos.

lessons.title: Sysmon process and network events
lessons.summary: Sysmon enriches Windows visibility. Event IDs depend on installed configuration, and not all endpoints collect all event types.
details: Sysmon 1 process creation; 3 network connection if enabled
Sysmon 7 image load, 11 file creation, 22 DNS query when configured
Parent and grandparent context often matter more than filename alone
workflow: Inspect process lineage, image path, hash and command line
Cross-check DNS and connection events for the same process GUID
Validate whether activity is normal on that host
lessons.example: winword.exe → powershell.exe → network connection is stronger evidence than powershell.exe alone.

lessons.title: Email headers and phishing
lessons.summary: Phishing investigations evaluate sender authentication, lookalike domains, URLs, attachments and user interaction. SPF, DKIM and DMARC outcomes are signals, not guarantees of safety.
details: SPF checks sending host authorization, DKIM checks cryptographic signature, DMARC aligns identities and sets policy
Display name can differ from envelope and header addresses
Check whether the user clicked, downloaded, entered credentials or approved MFA
workflow: Inspect full headers, URLs and attachment metadata
Search message trace for all recipients
Check sign-in activity after delivery and recommend containment
lessons.example: A payroll-themed message passes SPF but redirects through a new domain to a fake login page.

lessons.title: Firewall, proxy and DNS correlation
lessons.summary: One log source rarely tells the full story. Firewall indicates flows; proxy shows HTTP context; DNS shows attempted name resolution.
details: Blocked traffic does not establish a successful compromise
Allow/deny decisions need policy context
Proxy status and bytes can reveal transfers but require baselines
workflow: Start with source IP, destination and time window
Cross-check DNS resolution and proxy requests
Enrich with endpoint process and identity details
lessons.example: Suspicious DNS request followed by HTTPS POST and unusual uploaded bytes suggests deeper review.

lessons.title: EDR alerts and endpoint isolation
lessons.summary: Endpoint Detection and Response correlates processes, file and network behavior and offers containment actions. Isolation is impactful and usually requires approval.
details: EDR prevention events may show blocked execution with no successful compromise
Sensor offline does not mean host is clean
Isolation can disrupt servers and remote support
workflow: Read detection graph and prevention status
Check file, command line, persistence and lateral movement
Recommend approved containment with impact and rollback plan
lessons.example: An EDR alert says malicious script blocked; verify whether any child process or persistence succeeded before asserting containment.

lessons.title: Authentication and cloud sign-in logs
lessons.summary: Cloud and SaaS sign-in investigations require identity, device, application, conditional access and token context. Geolocation alone can be misleading.
details: VPN exits and mobile carriers create misleading travel patterns
Successful MFA may be attacker-induced through push fatigue or token theft
OAuth consent and app permissions can persist after password resets
workflow: Review interactive/noninteractive sign-ins and device trust
Check MFA details, consent grants and session history
Identify sensitive resources accessed after suspicious sign-in
lessons.example: A foreign IP sign-in via known corporate VPN on managed hardware may be benign; new app consent plus mailbox access is not.

lessons.title: What a SIEM really does
lessons.summary: A SIEM ingests and normalizes logs, enriches them, correlates events, and supports searches, alerts, dashboards and investigations. Garbage input creates bad detections.
details: SIEM is not a guarantee of complete coverage
Deduplication and parsing can lose fields
Detection rules have schedules, lookback windows and thresholds
workflow: Identify native data source and normalized schema
Explain rule conditions and suppression
Confirm searches use correct time range and fields
lessons.example: A correlation rule misses failures because source logs use username while normalized events use user.name.

lessons.title: Splunk SPL patterns
lessons.summary: SPL supports searching, transforming and aggregating machine data. Field names vary by sourcetype and environment.
details: index= and sourcetype= narrow the dataset
stats count by field groups events; where filters evaluated expressions
timechart shows time buckets; dedup and sort change displayed results
workflow: Start narrowly with index, timeframe and core indicator
Extract relevant fields and aggregate
Check raw events before interpreting summarized counts
lessons.example: index=windows EventCode=4625 | stats count by src_ip, user | sort - count

lessons.title: KQL fundamentals for Sentinel
lessons.summary: Kusto Query Language uses table expressions and operators such as where, project, extend, summarize and join. Table names depend on ingestion connector.
details: ago(1h) expresses a time filter; has and contains have different token semantics
summarize count() by groups rows; bin() buckets time
join can explode results when keys are not unique
workflow: Identify the target table and timestamp column
Filter early and project only needed fields
Aggregate, examine outliers and pivot into raw events
lessons.example: SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d) | summarize Failures=countif(ResultType != "0") by UserPrincipalName

lessons.title: Query pitfalls and baselines
lessons.summary: An outlier is not automatically malicious. High quality queries compare relevant periods, prevent wrong joins and handle case normalization.
details: Count unique hosts/users rather than just event volume when appropriate
Absence of logs can be a data gap instead of absence of activity
Overly broad regex and tiny time windows cause misleading results
workflow: Validate raw event counts and time range
Compare host role, shift hours and seasonal baseline
Document assumptions before converting searches to alerts
lessons.example: A backup server makes many SMB connections at 02:00; a workstation doing so for the first time is different.

lessons.title: Password spraying and brute force
lessons.summary: Spraying tests a few passwords across many accounts; brute force generally tests many candidates against one account. Detection depends on distribution and timeframe.
details: Distributed attacks can spread attempts across many IPs
Failures alone may reflect bad app configuration
Successes and MFA failures help raise confidence
workflow: Count distinct accounts per IP or ASN and time window
Compare success, lockouts and unusual devices
Check whether attacks are ongoing and protect exposed identities
lessons.example: One IP has three failures across 80 accounts followed by one success and a new MFA registration.

lessons.title: Suspicious PowerShell
lessons.summary: PowerShell is legitimate automation but also frequently abused. Analyze parent process, encoded input, network destinations and resulting behaviors without relying on one keyword.
details: -EncodedCommand may be used by benign management tools
Script block logging (4104) can show executed code if enabled
ExecutionPolicy is not a security boundary
workflow: Decode and inspect script content in a safe environment
Check parent-child lineage and script origin
Pivot into downloads, file writes, persistence and execution
lessons.example: A spreadsheet macro launching hidden PowerShell with a download command needs urgent review.

lessons.title: Malware, persistence and LOLBins
lessons.summary: Attackers may use scheduled tasks, services, startup folders and signed Windows tools for persistence or execution. Intent comes from behavior and context.
details: schtasks.exe and rundll32.exe have many valid uses
Registry Run keys and Windows services can establish persistence
One alert does not identify patient zero or full compromise scope
workflow: Check autoruns/tasks/services changed near execution
Investigate new files, parent process and signer
Search fleet for related file hash and behavior
lessons.example: A new task runs mshta.exe against an external URL each hour on a finance workstation.

lessons.title: Network scanning and lateral movement
lessons.summary: Scanning discovers targets; lateral movement uses access to other hosts. SMB, RDP, WinRM and remote service creation are common pivots, not proof on their own.
details: Scanning commonly shows many ports or destinations per source
Lateral movement often produces authentication and remote process artifacts
Maintenance tools and vulnerability scanners create similar noise
workflow: Check rate, target diversity and asset role
Join authentication events to network flow timeline
Look for remote execution or privilege changes
lessons.example: An ordinary desktop authenticates to 18 servers using one privileged credential at 03:00.

lessons.title: Web alerts and WAF triage
lessons.summary: Web Application Firewalls detect requests matching rule patterns. An alert may show a blocked probe, an application bug, or attempted exploitation.
details: Payload text is not proof the backend executed it
HTTP status 200 does not by itself prove successful SQL injection
Correlate WAF rule, upstream response, application log and server behavior
workflow: Inspect route, parameter, payload and response sequence
Determine blocked, challenged, forwarded or successful outcome
Search same source and target for later actions
lessons.example: Multiple traversal attempts blocked with 403 do not establish data theft; a later 200 plus file-access logs might.

lessons.title: IOC enrichment and reputation
lessons.summary: Reputation sources add context to IPs, domains, hashes and URLs but can be wrong or outdated. Do not upload private customer data to public scanners.
details: Shared hosting and CDNs make IP reputation unreliable alone
Hash reputation is exact-file specific and may miss variants
Passive DNS, WHOIS and domain age are context, not conclusions
workflow: Use approved intelligence services
Cross-check indicator with event behavior and timing
Record confidence, source, age and handling restrictions
lessons.example: An IOC feed labels a shared CDN IP malicious; the actual requested host belongs to a legitimate update service.

lessons.title: Writing incident summaries
lessons.summary: A good summary separates observations, assessment, impact and next steps. Use concise operational language and avoid unsupported certainty.
details: Evidence is what logs show; inference is what it may mean
Cite timestamps, time zones, accounts and hostnames consistently
Recommendations should have an owner, urgency and verification method
workflow: Open with incident type and current status
Describe timeline and confirmed impact
Note open questions and proposed actions
lessons.example: Observed: three anomalous logins; assessed: possible stolen credentials (medium confidence); action: revoke sessions pending IAM approval.

lessons.title: Hypothesis-driven investigations
lessons.summary: A hypothesis connects observations to a falsifiable explanation. L2 analysts should seek both supporting and disconfirming evidence to avoid tunnel vision.
details: The same activity can have competing benign and malicious explanations
A pivot should answer a specific investigative question
Keep an explicit distinction between not observed and ruled out
workflow: Write hypothesis and alternative explanation
Find independent data sources that can discriminate them
Update confidence as evidence appears
lessons.example: Hypothesis: attacker used VPN account for remote access; alternate: employee traveling; test device registration, ticket and access sequence.

lessons.title: Build a defensible incident timeline
lessons.summary: An incident timeline aligns endpoint, identity, network and cloud evidence. The goal is explaining sequence, scope and gaps, not only collecting IOCs.
details: UTC and raw timestamps must be preserved
Process IDs can be reused; GUIDs and start times improve joins
Log retention and late ingestion produce uncertainty
workflow: Create normalized chronological event list
Tag each event with source and reliability
Highlight initial access, execution, persistence, movement and impact
lessons.example: 08:01 phish delivered → 08:14 user clicked → 08:17 new sign-in → 08:23 inbox rule created.

lessons.title: Phishing-to-account-takeover chain
lessons.summary: Account takeover investigations span message delivery, credentials/session use, MFA, mailbox access, rules, OAuth grants and potential business email compromise.
details: Password reset alone may not invalidate existing tokens
Mailbox forwarding and app grants persist independently
A user can be the victim and an outbound phishing source
workflow: Search all recipients and clicks
Examine sign-ins, session/token artifacts and mailbox operations
Coordinate credential reset, session revocation and tenant cleanup
lessons.example: A fraudulent invoice message is followed by new forwarding rule and financial-team mailbox search.

lessons.title: Ransomware incident triage
lessons.summary: Potential ransomware demands quick containment coordination, proof collection and scoping. Do not disable forensic telemetry casually or assume one encrypted file means fleet-wide spread.
details: Mass file modification, shadow copy deletion and ransom notes are suspicious together
Backups and domain controller access change response urgency
Recovery choices belong to authorized incident leadership
workflow: Confirm process and affected hosts using EDR and file events
Determine spread and privileged access
Recommend containment, preserve artifacts and hand off to response lead
lessons.example: A file server shows thousands of renames, vssadmin execution and suspicious remote admin login.

lessons.title: Lateral movement reconstruction
lessons.summary: Track how an identity or process moved across systems, distinguishing legitimate administration from unauthorized use.
details: WinRM, PsExec-like services, RDP and SMB leave different evidence
Account use does not prove the human owner performed the action
Local and domain admin rights alter scope
workflow: Join authentication, EDR and network connection events
Trace source and destination hosts with time ordering
Identify credentials, sessions and systems requiring remediation
lessons.example: A stolen helpdesk token is used to launch a remote service on payroll and then a database host.

lessons.title: Cloud IAM and audit trails
lessons.summary: Cloud incident investigations examine identities, role assumptions, API calls, workload changes and data access. Logging may be account-, project- or region-specific.
details: AWS CloudTrail logs management operations; data events need relevant configuration
Azure activity and sign-in logs answer different questions
GCP Cloud Audit Logs distinguish activity categories and resource context
workflow: Determine principal, source IP, action, resource and result
Look for persistence via keys, policies or new identities
Scope storage reads, egress and role expansion
lessons.example: A workload key creates a new access key and exports data from a sensitive bucket.

lessons.title: DNS tunneling and C2 hypotheses
lessons.summary: Command-and-control can hide in seemingly normal web and DNS traffic. Analysts use periodicity, data volume and process correlation, not just a domain name.
details: High-entropy long labels and TXT records can be benign
Regular beacon intervals can arise from software updates
Tunneling claims require evidence of encoded traffic and transfer behavior
workflow: Group queries by source, domain and time
Check query lengths, record types, failures and periodicity
Correlate endpoint process with egress and proxy
lessons.example: An endpoint makes many long unique TXT queries to one unapproved domain immediately after script execution.

lessons.title: Threat intelligence and ATT&CK mapping
lessons.summary: Threat intelligence should inform a local testable hypothesis, not dictate attribution. ATT&CK mapping helps coverage review and evidence organization.
details: A shared tool or IP seldom identifies a specific threat group
Technique IDs should map to observed behavior
Confidence, source reliability and recency matter
workflow: Read report for behaviors and telemetry requirements
Hunt for the behavior in local environment
Document results, gaps and detection opportunities
lessons.example: A report describes scheduled-task persistence; hunt for newly registered tasks following suspicious script execution.

lessons.title: Containment, eradication and recovery
lessons.summary: Response balances stopping harm with business continuity and forensic needs. NIST SP 800-61r3 aligns response with CSF 2.0 and broader organizational risk management.
details: Containment isolates or limits activity; eradication removes cause and persistence
Recovery verifies clean return to service and monitoring
Decisions require delegated authority, legal/business coordination and rollback planning
workflow: Confirm incident scope and critical systems
Propose actions, dependencies and evidence preservation
Verify outcomes and search for recurrence
lessons.example: Before isolating a production domain controller, incident leadership evaluates continuity, scope and alternative containment.

lessons.title: Evidence preservation and chain of custody
lessons.summary: Evidence is useful only if investigators know its origin, integrity and handling. Practical SOC work emphasizes repeatable export, timestamps and restricted access.
details: Capture tool, operator, time, source, hash and storage location
Volatile state can disappear when systems reboot or isolate
Do not alter original evidence while analyzing copies
workflow: Record acquisition method and case reference
Hash exported artifacts where appropriate
Restrict access, preserve originals and document transfers
lessons.example: A memory image stored with SHA-256 and a signed transfer log is easier to defend than an untracked screenshot.

lessons.title: Incident communications and stakeholders
lessons.summary: Responders coordinate technical action with affected service owners, leadership, IAM, legal and communications. Reporting should be accurate and need-to-know.
details: Share confirmed facts and current uncertainty separately
Avoid naming perpetrators without supporting evidence
Choose update frequency based on severity and stakeholder needs
workflow: Issue initial status and impact summary
Track action owners and approvals
Provide updates, closure criteria and lessons learned
lessons.example: For suspected SaaS exfiltration, legal and data protection stakeholders are notified according to policy, not automatically by every L1 analyst.

lessons.title: Tuning noisy rules without losing coverage
lessons.summary: Detection tuning improves precision while preserving true-positive recall. A suppression should have owner, expiration and compensating visibility.
details: A whitelist based on one broad IP range is often risky
Precision=TP/(TP+FP); recall=TP/(TP+FN)
Sampling confirmed benign and malicious events helps evaluate changes
workflow: Collect true and false positive examples
Propose narrow exclusions with justification
Test against historical cases and monitor misses
lessons.example: Exclude only a signed enterprise updater on managed hosts, rather than all PowerShell executions.

lessons.title: Sigma rules and detection portability
lessons.summary: Sigma describes log detections in YAML with title, logsource, detection and optional metadata. Backends translate to platform-specific queries with field mapping limitations.
details: selection and condition express match logic
Logsource product/service/category describes expected telemetry
A Sigma rule is not automatically portable without schema and pipeline mapping
workflow: Identify required event source and fields
Write selection and condition
Test against real benign and malicious samples
lessons.example: A Sigma rule for suspicious service installation must verify the Windows Event ID and source-specific field names.

lessons.title: Structured threat hunting
lessons.summary: Hunting proactively tests a hypothesis against available telemetry, records gaps, and turns repeatable findings into detections. It is not simply running random IOC searches.
details: Intel-driven, hypothesis-driven and analytics-driven hunts start differently
Document scope, population, timeframe, exclusions and result
Negative findings are only meaningful when data coverage is adequate
workflow: Form a threat behavior hypothesis
Translate it to observable events and queries
Investigate hits, record gaps and propose new control
lessons.example: Hunt: unexpected process accesses LSASS on workstations during last 14 days; validate EDR telemetry retention first.

lessons.title: Behavioral analytics and anomalies
lessons.summary: Behavioral detections use peer groups, baselines, features and thresholds. An anomaly is a starting point for investigation, not a verdict.
details: Account role and host function matter to baselines
Rare does not mean malicious; common does not mean safe
Seasonality, data drift and missingness affect model output
workflow: Define feature and normal population
Build comparable time-based baseline
Validate anomalies using independent signals
lessons.example: A finance user normally downloads 30 MB/day; 8 GB to an unknown cloud host after suspicious OAuth grant changes the risk story.

lessons.title: Detection engineering lifecycle
lessons.summary: Engineering includes threat model, telemetry contract, query, test cases, deployment, monitoring and maintenance. Every detection needs an owner.
details: Detection-as-code enables review and version control
Simulated adversary tests can measure known behavior but not all evasions
Detection metadata should include ATT&CK mapping, triage guide and data dependencies
workflow: Write a clear behavioral hypothesis
Build and test representative positive/negative examples
Deploy with rollback and review alert quality
lessons.example: A rule identifies new remote services followed by suspicious binary execution, with automated unit examples and weekly false-positive review.

lessons.title: ATT&CK coverage gaps and purple teaming
lessons.summary: Coverage matrices expose which behaviors are detected and which are only logged or prevented. Purple teaming tests controls collaboratively with defined authorization.
details: A mapped rule is not evidence of effective coverage
Test design needs prerequisites, expected telemetry and success criteria
Document detections, misses, detection delay and remediation
workflow: Pick business-relevant threat scenario
Map expected behaviors and data sources
Run an approved safe test, review logs and improve rules
lessons.example: A sanctioned credential-access emulation tests whether an EDR alert reaches the SIEM and whether L1 can correctly triage it.

lessons.title: Digital forensics and memory concepts
lessons.summary: Host forensics connects disk artifacts, process state and volatile memory while preserving integrity. Analysts must know limitations and avoid unapproved collection.
details: RAM may contain process/network artifacts absent from disk
Prefetch, Amcache and Shimcache have caveats and cannot independently prove execution timing
Forensic images and timelines demand documented provenance
workflow: Define the investigative question before collecting
Choose appropriate volatile and nonvolatile artifacts
Correlate independent sources and articulate limitations
lessons.example: A suspicious executable was deleted; prefetch plus EDR and browser download records help reconstruct its activity.

lessons.title: Malware analysis workflow
lessons.summary: Malware triage progresses from metadata and static inspection to controlled dynamic analysis when authorized. Never run suspect samples on a normal workstation.
details: Hashes and signatures establish identity, not maliciousness
Imports, strings and sections offer hints but are easy to obfuscate
Behavioral sandbox observations require a suitable isolated environment
workflow: Preserve sample and hash in approved storage
Inspect metadata, strings and public reputation
Escalate to isolated dynamic analysis if permitted
lessons.example: A purported PDF is a Windows PE executable with suspicious import table and persistence behavior in a sandbox.

lessons.title: Identity attack paths and BloodHound
lessons.summary: Graph analysis maps how identities and privileges combine into reachable attack paths. Paths indicate opportunities and must be validated against live permissions and policy.
details: Attack paths depend on freshness of collection and scope
Nested group membership, delegation and local admin rights matter
Graph reachability alone does not prove an attacker exploited anything
workflow: Define target assets and privileged roles
Collect approved permissions and relationships
Prioritize choke points and remediation owners
lessons.example: A helpdesk group can reset password of an application owner with broad permissions; reduce unintended delegation.

lessons.title: Container and Kubernetes monitoring
lessons.summary: Containers share the host kernel; Kubernetes adds API, RBAC, admission, audit and workload concerns. SOC analysts correlate runtime alerts with deployment context.
details: Container image vulnerabilities do not prove runtime exploitation
Service accounts and Kubernetes RBAC can enable lateral movement
Runtime namespace/process behavior differs from host context
workflow: Identify pod, image digest, namespace and service account
Check API audit, container runtime and node events
Scope credentials and affected workloads
lessons.example: A pod with unexpected shell execution also makes Kubernetes API requests using a newly mounted token.

lessons.title: Cloud detection engineering
lessons.summary: Cloud detections should model API behavior, privilege context, expected infrastructure-as-code changes and account boundaries.
details: Role assumption, policy modifications and key creation are high-value behaviors
Legitimate CI/CD often performs sensitive API calls
Multi-account observability and log retention are frequent blind spots
workflow: Correlate principal, session and source network
Join changes to approved deployments and ticket IDs
Alert on suspicious sequence or unusual principal-context combination
lessons.example: A new access key is immediately used from an unseen ASN to disable audit logging and enumerate object storage.

lessons.title: Root cause analysis and post-incident review
lessons.summary: An effective review explains how the incident happened, why controls failed, and how improvements will be measured without blaming individuals.
details: Distinguish initial cause from contributing factors
Action items should be specific, owned and dated
Measure time-to-detect, time-to-contain and recurrence using clear definitions
workflow: Build factual timeline with evidence
Identify control and process gaps
Assign corrective actions, validation and follow-up
lessons.example: A phishing incident showed weak token revocation and insufficient audit retention; those become measurable engineering tasks.

lessons.title: Metrics, SLAs and SOC maturity
lessons.summary: Operational metrics should improve decisions, not reward premature closures. A high number of closed alerts can conceal poor detection quality.
details: MTTD and MTTR definitions depend on start/stop event rules
Backlog age, escalation quality and detection coverage add context
Precision and false-positive rate are different measures
workflow: Define metric and source consistently
Segment by severity and incident class
Review trends alongside case quality and missing telemetry
lessons.example: The team reduced alert queue by 40% but failed to detect identity compromise due to disabled log ingestion: a misleading success.

lessons.title: Threat modeling and architecture review
lessons.summary: Threat models connect business assets, trust boundaries, potential attacker actions and feasible controls. SOC feedback should shape architecture.
details: Data flows expose choke points and logging needs
STRIDE is one model for categorizing threat types
Trust boundaries and privilege transitions are good places for detection controls
workflow: Draw assets, identities and data flows
Identify attacker objectives and abuse paths
Propose prioritized prevention, logging and detections
lessons.example: A public upload API can store files in cloud storage; model unauthenticated input, scanning, IAM and audit trail requirements.

lessons.title: Packet journey: from browser to server
lessons.summary: Trace a request through DNS resolution, TCP/TLS setup, routing, load balancers, and application logs. A single failure can leave evidence in several layers.
details: Client resolves name before connecting unless cached or pinned
TCP SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK establishes a session; UDP has no such handshake
Reverse proxies and NAT can change the IP observed by application logs
workflow: State which hostname and destination were used
Examine resolver, firewall and proxy visibility separately
Reconstruct the request order in one timezone
lessons.example: The edge firewall allows TCP/443, but the web app rejects the request at authentication; network allow does not imply application success.
evidence: DNS qname, proxy URI/status, firewall 5-tuple
Client IP versus forwarded IP provenance
pitfalls: Treating a port as proof of protocol
Calling a dropped SYN an HTTP error

lessons.title: DNS records and investigation pivots
lessons.summary: Understand A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, NS, PTR, TTL, NXDOMAIN and recursive versus authoritative answers. DNS events help form—but rarely prove—a C2 hypothesis.
details: A/AAAA resolve names; CNAME aliases to another name
MX routes mail; TXT includes SPF and ownership signals
Caching and TTL mean observations may differ over time
workflow: Determine which client and resolver made a query
Group by domain, client, response code and interval
Correlate the requesting process and subsequent connections
lessons.example: Four TXT lookups with changing subdomain labels from one endpoint warrant comparison with normal software update behavior.
evidence: Query type, answer, TTL, rcode and resolver
Endpoint process-to-DNS association
pitfalls: Assuming NXDOMAIN equals compromise
Blocking a domain without business impact review

lessons.title: DHCP, ARP, VLANs and switch telemetry
lessons.summary: Place a security event on the correct local-network segment; know why host IP and MAC mappings change and why VLAN boundaries matter.
details: DHCP leases assign addresses with expiry and reassignment
ARP resolves local IPv4 neighbors; IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery
VLANs separate broadcast domains while routed traffic crosses L3 controls
workflow: Find asset identity at the event timestamp
Correlate DHCP lease, switchport, NAC and VPN records
Note NAT, shared IP and virtual NIC ambiguity
lessons.example: A firewall log gives 10.4.5.19 at 01:10 UTC; the DHCP lease proves it belonged to a kiosk then, not the laptop using it at noon.
evidence: DHCP client MAC and lease interval
Switch port, NAC identity and VLAN
pitfalls: Using current IP-to-device inventory for historical attribution
Treating a MAC as globally unique identity

lessons.title: Email delivery and authentication
lessons.summary: Read SMTP hop evidence, envelope sender, From header, Reply-To, SPF, DKIM, and DMARC alignment without assuming an authenticated message is safe.
details: SPF validates authorized sending IP against envelope identities
DKIM verifies signed header/body portions and a domain signature
DMARC uses alignment and policy; pass does not certify sender intent
workflow: Trace Received headers in plausible order
Compare visible sender to envelope and Reply-To
Combine attachment behavior, URLs and user action
lessons.example: A phishing message sent from a compromised legitimate vendor can pass all three controls.
evidence: Message-ID, authentication-results and attachment hash
URL clicks, recipient actions and mailbox rules
pitfalls: Calling SPF pass a clean verdict
Trusting external display names

lessons.title: Windows logon type decision map
lessons.summary: Security Event 4624 records successful logons; the LogonType and account context shape whether it represents an interactive login, remote network use or a service.
details: Type 2 interactive, type 3 network, type 10 remote interactive
Type 4 batch and type 5 service can be routine
Correlate 4624 with 4625, 4634, 4648, 4672 and host role
workflow: Read TargetUserName, LogonType, IpAddress and LogonId
Compare logon origin with endpoint inventory and admin schedule
Pivot to new processes, shares, service creation or RDP activity
lessons.example: Type 3 on a file server is normal until paired with a privileged account and a new service installed minutes later.
evidence: 4624 LogonType/LogonId fields
7045, Sysmon 1 and EDR process tree
pitfalls: Mistaking type 3 for RDP
Treating 4672 alone as proof of escalation

lessons.title: Windows event channels and audit coverage
lessons.summary: Distinguish Security, System, PowerShell Operational, Sysmon, and Defender/EDR telemetry; absence of events can be a collection-policy problem.
details: Security shows audited logon, object and account events
System includes service events and platform errors
PowerShell logging depends on policies and may expose different details than Sysmon
workflow: Confirm source channel and collection health
Look up exact event semantics and logging policy
Cross-check with another sensor when coverage is incomplete
lessons.example: An endpoint shows Sysmon 1 but no PowerShell 4104 because script-block logging is disabled; do not infer no scripts executed.
evidence: EventID, channel, provider, host and record ID
GPO audit policy and connector heartbeat
pitfalls: Concluding a system is clean from a missing event
Confusing Sysmon and Security Event IDs

lessons.title: Linux authentication and auditd essentials
lessons.summary: Understand SSH, sudo, su, journald, auth logs, cron/systemd and auditd context so Linux hosts are not treated as blind spots.
details: Systemd journal centralizes many services; distro log files vary
SSH authentication successes and failures need source and account context
auditd can capture process/file access when configured
workflow: Verify local time and daemon/source
Compare SSH success with sudo, session and service modifications
Find persistence in authorized_keys, cron and systemd units
lessons.example: Repeated SSH failures followed by success are not enough to label compromise without account ownership and subsequent commands.
evidence: journalctl entries, sshd logs and auditd execve
systemd timer/service changes and file hashes
pitfalls: Assuming /var/log/auth.log exists on every distro
Treating root sudo as always suspicious

lessons.title: Authentication protocols: OAuth/OIDC/SAML
lessons.summary: Know the roles of identity provider, service provider, tokens, assertions, scopes, claims and consent; understand what sign-in logs can and cannot reveal.
details: SAML commonly exchanges signed assertions between IdP and service
OIDC builds identity on OAuth 2.0 token flows
Refresh/access tokens have different uses and lifetime controls
workflow: Identify whether the event is an interactive sign-in, token refresh or app-only grant
Examine application, token audience and permission scope
Correlate consent and privileged audit events
lessons.example: A user consent grant to an unknown app with mail.read scope may persist after a password change.
evidence: App ID, service principal, consent event and scopes
Device, session and token issuance metadata
pitfalls: Calling every access token an ID token
Assuming MFA reappears for each refresh

lessons.title: Kerberos and NTLM in SOC investigations
lessons.summary: Read domain authentication patterns and distinguish ticket-granting behavior from password failures while respecting local audit-policy dependencies.
details: Kerberos AS/TGS flows have different service purposes
Events 4768, 4769, 4771 and 4776 answer different questions
NTLM still appears in legacy environments and requires risk context
workflow: Identify principal, source workstation and service name
Check ticket patterns and account permissions
Pivot to DC logs plus endpoint processes and network flow
lessons.example: Many TGS requests for privileged service accounts may merit review, but regular application activity can be similarly noisy.
evidence: DC Security 4768/4769 and SPN
Source process, encryption-type context and approved services
pitfalls: Assuming ticket requests alone equal credential theft
Treating 4771 as a general successful logon

lessons.title: Encoding, encryption, hashing and signatures
lessons.summary: Separate reversible encoding, secret-key encryption, one-way hashing, keyed MACs and public-key signatures. Analysts often see these in malware, TLS and artifact validation.
details: Base64 is encoding, not confidentiality
Hashes summarize content; collisions and changes have different meanings
Digital signatures prove a signer key was used, not that a signed program is safe
workflow: Classify which primitive an artifact actually uses
Preserve original bytes before decoding
Verify hash/signature provenance and compare with trusted baselines
lessons.example: A signed installer from a compromised vendor can still behave maliciously; correlate signer with reputation and process behavior.
evidence: SHA-256 digest and file metadata
Signature chain, certificate status and timestamp
pitfalls: Calling Base64 encryption
Labeling any signed binary benign

lessons.title: Risk, CVSS, EPSS and exploit evidence
lessons.summary: Prioritize vulnerabilities using exposure, exploitability, business criticality and active exploitation rather than a score in isolation.
details: CVSS describes severity characteristics, not actual compromise
EPSS estimates exploitation probability and is not an incident verdict
Internet reachability and compensating controls matter
workflow: Confirm asset, version and vulnerable component
Check exposure and known exploitation evidence
Assign remediation owner and verification date
lessons.example: A critical library in a disconnected test environment may rank below an actively exploited internet-facing medium-severity flaw.
evidence: Asset inventory and version evidence
Vulnerability scan details and patch status
pitfalls: Treating CVSS 10 as automatic active breach
Declaring patch complete without rescanning

lessons.title: Data formats: JSON, CSV, Syslog and ECS
lessons.summary: Understand parsers, field extraction, normalization and ingestion delays. Query errors often begin at data-shape assumptions.
details: JSON nesting and field types determine query syntax
Syslog header conventions vary by sender and format
ECS/ASIM-like schemas help normalize disparate products
workflow: Inspect a raw example and field mappings
Compare parsed time with original timestamp
Validate null/missing fields and dropped events
lessons.example: An IP is stored under client.ip in one index and src_ip in another; a query can silently miss half the fleet.
evidence: Raw log and parsed fields side by side
Ingest timestamp versus event timestamp
pitfalls: Assuming identical fields across vendors
Silently casting invalid timestamps

lessons.title: Cloud shared responsibility model
lessons.summary: Know which layer the provider secures and which configurations, identities, data and applications remain the customer’s responsibility.
details: IaaS requires guest OS and application hardening
Managed services shift operational tasks but not data classification
Audit coverage depends on cloud-specific log configuration
workflow: Identify the cloud service and security boundary
Check IAM, logging and network configuration
Recommend controls owned by the correct team
lessons.example: An exposed object storage bucket is often a tenant configuration issue, not evidence of provider infrastructure compromise.
evidence: IAM policy, bucket permissions and cloud audit trail
Provider status and tenant configuration history
pitfalls: Assuming managed means automatically secure
Confusing service health with account security

lessons.title: ATT&CK tactics versus techniques versus detection
lessons.summary: Use ATT&CK as a behavioral map rather than an automatic attribution engine; one event may support multiple hypotheses.
details: Tactics express goals; techniques describe behaviors
A technique ID is not a malware family or attacker identity
Mapping requires actual evidence, not guesses from alert titles
workflow: Describe exact observed behavior
Map at the narrowest supported technique level
Record telemetry gaps and alternative explanations
lessons.example: Service creation with a temporary binary can support remote execution hypotheses but does not independently identify an operator.
evidence: Observed command/process/service data
Detection rule and technique rationale
pitfalls: Overmapping every stage of an attack chain
Inferring nation-state actor from a single technique

lessons.title: SLA clock, queue ownership and handover
lessons.summary: Treat an alert as owned work: deadline, state, next action and escalation are distinct fields. Duplicate cases should link without erasing evidence.
details: Severity does not always equal urgency; critical assets change priority
SLA breach risk grows when ownership is ambiguous
Handover must include status and blockers, not only ticket link
workflow: Identify priority and response policy
Assign owner and record next check time
Escalate pending decisions before shift change
lessons.example: Two analysts both assume the other contacted the asset owner; a precise handover prevents the gap.
evidence: Ticket created/updated timestamps and assigned responder
Decision record and contact attempts
pitfalls: Closing on assignment without investigation
Unowned P1 alerts during shift handover

lessons.title: Distinguish detections, events, incidents and cases
lessons.summary: An event is observation; a detection correlates observations into a signal; an incident is validated security harm or policy-significant activity according to organizational criteria.
details: A true positive detection can be authorized activity
A case can combine many alerts around one entity/timeframe
Escalation is based on confidence and impact, not alert volume
workflow: Validate alert logic and supporting events
Check intent, authorization and business context
Disposition with a clear evidence-backed explanation
lessons.example: A managed vulnerability scanner triggers a port-scan rule; the behavior is real but approved in a change window.
evidence: Alert rule logic and raw matching events
Change ticket and relevant asset owner
pitfalls: Calling every rule match an incident
Calling a benign positive a false positive

lessons.title: Security event 4688 and command-line visibility
lessons.summary: Event 4688 can record process creation, depending on audit settings; full command-line collection is controlled separately. Sysmon Event 1 often provides additional context.
details: Read creator process, account, image and command line if logged
Parent and child sequence reveals suspicious application-to-shell chains
Process IDs can be reused and need time and entity context
workflow: Verify 4688 audit policy and source host
Build process tree around suspicious execution
Check signer, child processes and subsequent network actions
lessons.example: winword.exe launching powershell.exe with encoded command is suspicious context, not a proof of decoded intent.
evidence: 4688 NewProcessName/CommandLine
Sysmon 1 ProcessGuid and parent data
pitfalls: Assuming every 4688 has arguments
Correlating reused PID across hours

lessons.title: Account creation, group membership and privilege changes
lessons.summary: Learn common Windows and AD event IDs used to identify new accounts and group changes; distinguish local and domain scopes.
details: 4720 account created, 4726 deleted and 4738 changed
4728/4732/4756 cover additions to different group scopes
Audit location and event fields vary; privileged membership needs immediate context
workflow: Confirm acting principal and target account
Compare change windows and approved requests
Identify new privileges and correlated sign-ins
lessons.example: An unplanned addition to Domain Admins after suspicious login is a high-priority escalation, even if EDR has no malware alert.
evidence: DC Security log member-change event
Group SID, actor, ticket and target
pitfalls: Mixing up group scope event IDs
Ignoring who performed the change

lessons.title: Phishing URL and attachment investigation
lessons.summary: Investigate message, recipient, click, download and execution as separate facts; do not detonate untrusted artifacts on a workstation.
details: Differentiate delivery, click and execution
URL redirects may change destination after delivery
Safe reputation and sandbox services have privacy and authorization limits
workflow: Preserve message identifiers and headers
Search mail gateway and proxy for clicks
Use EDR to confirm process execution and affected scope
lessons.example: A blocked .exe after a click is not the same as successful malware execution; report delivered/clicked/blocked distinctly.
evidence: Email delivery status and recipient list
Proxy URL, EDR prevention event and process tree
pitfalls: Opening unknown attachments to check manually
Declaring compromise from email delivery alone

lessons.title: Business email compromise first response
lessons.summary: BEC often involves legitimate sessions, mailbox rules, payment requests or app grants; payload scanning alone will miss it.
details: Invoice urgency is a social-engineering cue, not proof
Forwarding rules and changed recovery methods increase risk
Token-based sessions can survive password changes
workflow: Compare conversation history and sender identity
Review mailbox audit and sign-ins
Escalate financial action and preserve records
lessons.example: A seemingly normal vendor requests a new bank account; finance should verify through an independently known channel.
evidence: Audit New-InboxRule/Set-Mailbox and sign-in locations
Payment change and mail access timeline
pitfalls: Using reply-to-email for verification
Assuming no malware means no BEC

lessons.title: EDR alert action versus observed outcome
lessons.summary: EDR may alert, quarantine a file, kill a process or isolate host. Analysts must separate intended control action from confirmed execution results.
details: Blocked execution does not guarantee no earlier activity
Suspicious child process requires tracing its ancestors
Sensor gaps and tamper events reduce confidence
workflow: Read action and action result fields
Check pre-detection and post-detection process activity
Verify whether isolation/quarantine actually completed
lessons.example: An alert-only detection with a persistent outbound connection is more urgent than a blocked file with no child processes.
evidence: Alert classification, action result and process GUID
Sensor last-seen time and network artifacts
pitfalls: Calling alert_only blocked
Missing alternative execution paths

lessons.title: HTTP redirects, proxies and web request attribution
lessons.summary: Understand the difference between proxy logs, WAF events, application outcomes and browser sessions. HTTP 200 does not necessarily mean authorized action.
details: A redirect can chain across hosts/domains
WAF action=block may preclude app execution for that request
NAT and reverse proxies complicate user attribution
workflow: Trace user/device to proxy request
Correlate WAF request ID with application response
Inspect upstream status and authenticated principal
lessons.example: A WAF detects traversal and blocks with 403 while the subsequent app request returns 200 for a benign report; do not conflate them.
evidence: WAF action, request ID and normalized URL
Application authorization result and proxy username
pitfalls: Treating every 200 response as data theft
Mistaking WAF detection for successful exploit

lessons.title: Field extraction, lookup tables and data models
lessons.summary: Searchable data depends on sourcetypes, parsing rules, schema mapping, enrichment freshness and retention; validate before building a rule.
details: Field types and casing may differ across indexes
Lookups can enrich with asset owner but become stale
Query time windows must account for ingestion delay
workflow: Inspect sample raw logs and extracted fields
Validate against known ground-truth events
Check lookup join coverage and unknown matches
lessons.example: A failed-logon dashboard suddenly drops to zero after a parser update; ingestion health matters more than celebrating the decline.
evidence: Raw message, source type and index lag
Lookup unmatched counts
pitfalls: Assuming visual dashboard implies complete coverage
Silently dropping null fields

lessons.title: Baseline and threshold alerts
lessons.summary: Baselines capture expected behavior, but an average can hide high variance and seasonality. A threshold is only a starting detection hypothesis.
details: Partition baselines by host role, user and time of day
Consider scheduled admin activity and maintenance windows
Rare events are not necessarily malicious; malicious can be common
workflow: Document what normal means for the entity
Compare current rate with cohort and historical windows
Pivot to process/account behavior before disposition
lessons.example: Ten failed logins may be severe for a rarely used service account but routine on an internet-facing auth gateway.
evidence: Hourly aggregates, host cohort and day-of-week
Source IP diversity and success-after-failure pattern
pitfalls: Using one global threshold for all asset classes
Auto-whitelisting noisy users

lessons.title: MFA fatigue, session anomaly and token theft
lessons.summary: Interpret push approval spam, new device registration, suspicious refresh tokens and post-authentication actions without conflating them.
details: MFA success alone does not validate session legitimacy
Token theft may not generate a new password attempt
Session revocation may be needed after account takeover
workflow: Inspect authentication method and device posture
Correlate sign-in and mailbox/cloud actions
Escalate credible compromise for approved session and account response
lessons.example: Repeated push denials followed by one approval and inbox forwarding change support account takeover concern.
evidence: MFA details, device compliance and app sessions
Authentication audit and token/consent activity
pitfalls: Treating a successful MFA as proof of safety
Resetting password without reviewing active sessions

lessons.title: Analyst ticket with confidence and uncertainty
lessons.summary: Write reproducible notes: who, what, when (UTC), where, evidence, assessment, actions and unknowns. Confidence is not the same as severity.
details: State a fact from evidence separately from a hypothesis
Use timestamps, log source and asset IDs
Explain why a containment request is proportionate to business impact
workflow: Write a two-sentence summary first
Attach concise supporting artifacts and negative findings
Identify owner and explicitly requested next step
lessons.example: Observed 4624 type 3 from unknown IP, then 7045 on host; suspected lateral movement, not confirmed exfiltration.
evidence: Raw event reference, detection rule and affected entities
Timeline and pending validation actions
pitfalls: Writing confirmed compromise without proof
Saying investigated and closed without rationale

lessons.title: SOC shift communications and fatigue management
lessons.summary: Protect handover quality during high-volume shifts with triage batches, explicit priorities and rest-aware double checks on disruptive actions.
details: High alert volume increases context-switching errors
Reliable templated notes beat memory
P1 incidents require designated communications cadence
workflow: Triage urgent, high-confidence business impact first
Group related alerts by entity/time to avoid duplicate work
Ask for peer review before high-impact emergency changes
lessons.example: A thousand matching scans share one approved scanner: link alert grouping and retain original evidence for an auditable suppression proposal.
evidence: Case status, SLA and alert grouping criteria
Handover acknowledgement and last update
pitfalls: Treating all alerts FIFO regardless of risk
Making isolation decisions while distracted without verification

lessons.title: Build process trees across Sysmon and EDR
lessons.summary: Correlate endpoint execution via ProcessGuid, parent relationships, users, hashes and timestamps. PID alone may be reused, and event ordering may be delayed.
details: Sysmon Event 1 records process creation when configured
Sysmon 3 network connection depends on configuration
Parent-child links and command line give stronger context than process name
workflow: Anchor on suspicious process GUID and start time
Expand parents, children and network connections
Confirm file origin, signer and persistence artifacts
lessons.example: Office spawning script interpreter and unusual HTTPS connection warrants host investigation despite common Windows binaries.
evidence: ProcessGuid, ParentProcessGuid and hash
Network five-tuple and related file writes
pitfalls: Using PID as durable identity
Assuming a signed interpreter is safe

lessons.title: Active Directory lateral movement investigation
lessons.summary: Reconstruct source-to-target movement using remote logons, service tasks, privileged accounts and network pivot evidence; distinguish admin work from intrusions.
details: 4624 type 3 plus 7045 can indicate remote service execution
Scheduled task events can show alternative remote execution
Domain controllers provide account context, but endpoints reveal actions
workflow: Collect origins, destinations and account context
Compare authentication to remote process/service evidence
Map exact affected hosts and privileged credentials
lessons.example: Same admin account creates an unfamiliar service on two hosts within minutes; check authorized deployment work before attribution.
evidence: 4624/4648, 7045 and network share access
EDR command line, service binary hash and change records
pitfalls: Assuming SMB alone implies lateral movement
Ignoring service account compromise

lessons.title: Kerberoasting detection and response
lessons.summary: Investigate unusual service-ticket acquisition patterns without depending on encryption type alone; privileged service accounts and post-auth events determine risk.
details: SPN-backed accounts may be targeted for offline password guessing
Event 4769 request rate and source matter
RC4 usage alone is not confirmation of attack
workflow: Build per-principal SPN/ticket baseline
Look for unusual bursts and affected sensitive accounts
Recommend credential hygiene and identity response by policy
lessons.example: A single app server requesting usual SQL service tickets should not be escalated as proven Kerberoasting.
evidence: 4769 service name, client address and encryption info
SPN inventory and privilege of target account
pitfalls: Treating ticket volume as stolen password proof
Disabling production service accounts without approval

lessons.title: DCSync and directory replication anomalies
lessons.summary: Monitor directory replication privilege abuse using security events and DC role context; legitimate DC replication must not be confused with abuse.
details: Directory replication rights may be held outside domain controllers
Access event 4662 requires suitable SACL and audit setup
Non-DC sources requesting replication are an investigation lead
workflow: Verify audit coverage and principal replication rights
Correlate 4662 with host identity and network session
Escalate confirmed unauthorized privilege for coordinated credential response
lessons.example: A backup server with delegated rights may generate replication-like activity; ownership validation prevents damaging containment.
evidence: 4662 properties/object context and account
Directory ACL changes and source host role
pitfalls: Claiming DCSync from 4662 alone
Ignoring SACL and domain-controller baseline

lessons.title: Windows persistence: tasks, services, Run keys and WMI
lessons.summary: Look beyond malware filename to persistence mechanisms and their creator, trigger, binary and authorization context.
details: Scheduled task and service creation are common admin methods
Registry Run keys may start programs at logon
WMI event subscriptions can persist and need specialist telemetry
workflow: Inspect new persistence object and creation time
Identify creator account and target image path
Compare with change history and process tree
lessons.example: A service pointing to a temporary user directory after an unusual remote logon merits escalation, not automatic deletion.
evidence: 7045, task-creation events and registry changes
EDR process tree and binary provenance
pitfalls: Removing evidence before preservation
Labeling every new scheduled task malicious

lessons.title: Data exfiltration scoping
lessons.summary: Determine whether bytes left, what data was accessible and whether uploads reached a destination. DNS or firewall counts alone cannot prove content transfer.
details: Traffic bytes may include protocol overhead and retries
Cloud audit data events may require explicit configuration
Proxy and DLP logs offer different attribution strengths
workflow: Identify destination and initiating principal/process
Correlate storage access with transfer volume and success
Escalate potential data exposure with explicit uncertainty
lessons.example: Seventy-five GetObject events show file reads, not necessarily public disclosure; investigate principal, destination and approved workflows.
evidence: Object API audit, DLP and proxy upload metrics
Sensitive-data label and access grant timeline
pitfalls: Calling any high byte count confirmed theft
Relying on blocked firewall attempts as successful transfer

lessons.title: DNS beaconing and tunneling deep dive
lessons.summary: Assess inter-arrival regularity, domains, qtypes and payload shape alongside endpoint process and approved applications.
details: Regular polling can be benign scheduled software
High-entropy labels and excessive TXT queries are leads
Passive DNS does not give payload meaning with encrypted DNS
workflow: Establish host baseline and parent process
Quantify query distribution and interval variance
Compare destinations, reputation, ownership and process behavior
lessons.example: A laptop making TXT queries every 60 seconds may be a sync client; the unmanaged binary and domain novelty are needed for stronger suspicion.
evidence: DNS request times, qtype/rcode and unique subdomains
Sysmon process-to-network events and proxy metadata
pitfalls: Declaring C2 solely from 60-second interval
Assuming entropy alone proves data encoding

lessons.title: Containment choices and business blast radius
lessons.summary: Balance stopping ongoing harm against operational damage: account disablement, session revocation, host isolation and network blocks target different scopes.
details: Isolation may sever response access on critical endpoints
Disabling a service account can break business workflows
A block may not revoke existing tokens or sessions
workflow: Identify active threat and containment objective
Obtain authorization and fallback/rollback plan
Verify containment action succeeded and monitor for alternatives
lessons.example: For an actively encrypting workstation, approved isolation may be urgent; a database cluster needs explicit coordinated response.
evidence: EDR action result, IAM session audit and firewall change
Change ticket and validation telemetry
pitfalls: Issuing unapproved disruptive commands
Equating requested action with successful containment

lessons.title: Incident timeline and chain of evidence
lessons.summary: Combine disparate logs using UTC, original timezones, collection delays, source fidelity and notes about contradictions; preserve raw artifacts.
details: A SIEM ingest time can be later than event creation
Endpoint clocks may drift and misorder sequences
Hashes and custody records protect reproducibility, not absolute truth
workflow: Capture original timestamp and source clock context
Build a sorted timeline with confidence levels
Record evidence origin, storage and analysts handling it
lessons.example: Mail delivery 08:01, click 08:03, session 08:05 and rule change 08:07 form a hypothesis requiring account audit confirmation.
evidence: Message ID, sign-in ID and event timestamps
Evidence hash, acquisition method and custody record
pitfalls: Mixing local and UTC silently
Changing a source artifact while annotating

lessons.title: Ransomware: precursor versus impact
lessons.summary: Identify stages such as suspicious authentication, backup tampering, mass encryption and ransom notes; distinguish high-confidence impact from a single tool invocation.
details: vssadmin activity can be legitimate backup admin work
File-renaming spikes and ransom notes strongly elevate urgency
Scope includes shares, hypervisors, identity and backup integrity
workflow: Confirm affected host(s) and active encryption
Trigger approved crisis escalation and containment
Preserve evidence and coordinate recovery validation
lessons.example: Mass renamed files, ransom-note creation and unblocked suspicious process show likely active impact requiring urgent response.
evidence: EDR commands and event timeline
File-server I/O anomalies and backup integrity status
pitfalls: Waiting for antivirus signature in active encryption
Deleting notes and binaries before collection

lessons.title: Cloud compromise: AWS and Azure investigation
lessons.summary: Distinguish management-plane changes, data access and identity evidence; enumerate affected resource policies, tokens and key material.
details: CloudTrail management and data event coverage differ
Azure activity logs and Entra audit logs serve different purposes
Temporary role sessions can outlive an initial sign-in
workflow: Identify effective principal and assumed role/session
Map privilege changes and data-resource access
Revoke/rotate credentials under approved playbook and verify
lessons.example: CreateAccessKey followed by AdministratorAccess and unusual object reads is suspicious even when no endpoint is infected.
