evidence: Cloud audit eventName, principalArn and source IP
IAM policy history, app grants and object access events
pitfalls: Assuming a public IP means public cloud compromise
Confusing management access with data read completion

lessons.title: Incident communications for executives and legal
lessons.summary: Report scope, impact, containment, unknowns and decision points with appropriate confidence; avoid premature claims and preserve privacy.
details: Operational update differs from breach notification
Legal/privacy reporting depends on jurisdiction and evidence
Every update should name a next review time and decision owner
workflow: Draft verified facts and a separate hypotheses section
Explain affected business functions and current mitigations
Route external statements through incident leadership and legal
lessons.example: We observed unauthorized mailbox rules on one account; investigation is ongoing into downstream data access.
evidence: Case timeline and confirmed action record
Asset/data owner and required approvals
pitfalls: Stating no data loss before examining logs
Sending incident artifacts to unauthorized chat rooms

lessons.title: Sigma translation and field compatibility
lessons.summary: Translate generic detection logic into target SIEM fields with explicit parser mappings, null handling and validation using known-positive and known-benign logs.
details: Sigma selection/condition is abstract until backend translation
Field aliases and wildcard behavior vary
Query portability does not guarantee comparable data completeness
workflow: Write detection hypothesis and data prerequisites
Map fields for each target environment
Replay positive and negative scenarios and track coverage
lessons.example: An impossible-travel Sigma-style rule still needs identity provider device context and VPN exit labels in the SIEM.
evidence: Rule YAML and backend query
Test events, false-positive log and deployment history
pitfalls: Copying Sigma YAML into SPL without translation
Ignoring source event schema

lessons.title: Triage rule QA and alert suppression
lessons.summary: Tune detections with safe, narrow exceptions that preserve uncommon malicious behavior; measure precision and recall on reviewed datasets.
details: Suppression can hide the same behavior from an attacker
Allowlists should have owner and expiry
Precision improves only when benign population is understood
workflow: Review 30–90 days matched alert examples
Add context: signer, parent, asset role and change window
Replay adversarial test and measure false negatives
lessons.example: Exclude a known scanner only when hostname, owner and approved time range match; keep detections for that account elsewhere.
evidence: Rule versions and sample match counts
Approved tuning exceptions and expiry
pitfalls: Whitelisting an IP range forever
Optimizing only for alert volume

lessons.title: Hunt hypothesis: lateral movement with remote services
lessons.summary: Design a testable hypothesis around cross-host authentication and short-lived service creation, then hunt at scale without equating every admin tool with intrusion.
details: Hypotheses should specify population, timeframe and signals
Known admins and deployment tools form a comparison cohort
A missing source weakens conclusions, it is not proof of absence
workflow: State hypothesis and required 4624/7045 telemetry
Join accounts, origins, targets and creation intervals
Investigate rare clusters; document counterexamples and findings
lessons.example: A service installed on three servers by a new admin origin is a lead; maintenance records may resolve it benign.
evidence: Normalized 4624 source/workstation and 7045 binary
Host inventory, EDR and deployment schedule
pitfalls: Using a global service-creation threshold
Reporting a hunt as no threats without coverage caveat

lessons.title: Hunt hypothesis: suspicious OAuth consent
lessons.summary: Correlate new application consent, broad scopes, unusual principals and subsequent API operations; identity-only threats may not involve endpoint malware.
details: User-consent policy changes attack surface
Mail.Read, offline_access and admin grants can alter risk
App permissions need tenant and owner context
workflow: Find recent consent grants and app registrations
Enrich publisher, scope, signer and approval history
Pivot to app-only and delegated API reads
lessons.example: An unknown app obtains offline_access and Mail.Read then accesses unusual mailboxes; remove consent only under authorized response.
evidence: Consent audit, servicePrincipal ID and API calls
Application owner and approval ticket
pitfalls: Treating all third-party apps malicious
Resetting user passwords as only mitigation

lessons.title: Statistical beacon detection
lessons.summary: Use interval variance, periodograms or time-binned counts to surface regular external callbacks, then validate service schedules and endpoint processes.
details: Fixed cadence is a clue, not malicious proof
Clock jitter and batching distort inter-arrival stats
Scoring should include rare destinations and execution context
workflow: Build per host/destination time series
Compare to benign update cohorts
Review process lineage and domain age with privacy controls
lessons.example: A 5-minute heartbeat to a signed updater is normal; a new unsigned binary calling an unrecognized domain is not.
evidence: Flow timestamps, byte trends and destination
Process image, signed status and user context
pitfalls: Conflating NTP and C2 polling
Ignoring sampling and NAT bias

lessons.title: ATT&CK coverage matrix and data-source gaps
lessons.summary: Separate detection-rule existence from telemetry coverage and analytic validation; treat an unmonitored technique as unknown rather than safe.
details: Technique overlap does not imply all sub-techniques covered
Rules depend on quality and retention of required data
Control testing establishes measurable confidence
workflow: Select priority threats for business assets
Map available telemetry and rules to tested technique behaviors
Record gaps, owner, risk and next validation exercise
lessons.example: A service-creation rule on half the endpoint fleet does not provide full lateral movement coverage.
evidence: Sensor inventory and event volumes by host
Tested attack emulation outcomes and rule mapping
pitfalls: Claiming percentage coverage by counting tags
Ignoring collection outages

lessons.title: Detection-as-code engineering workflow
lessons.summary: Treat analytics rules like production software: version control, peer review, tests, staging, metrics and rollback plans.
details: Queries can exceed SIEM performance limits
Rule naming and MITRE tags are documentation, not validation
A good rule should explain response and data prerequisites
workflow: Write hypothesis, prerequisites and detection query
Validate on synthetic positive and realistic benign negatives
Roll out gradually, monitor alert quality and revert if needed
lessons.example: A new command-line rule fires on backup tooling; narrow by signed parent and context instead of dropping the technique entirely.
evidence: Git diff, test cases, rule changelog
Query cost, false-positive and false-negative review
pitfalls: Deploying an untested detection globally
Optimizing speed by removing investigative fields

lessons.title: Structured detection QA metrics
lessons.summary: Measure true-positive yield, false-positive burden, median time to triage and gap-specific coverage without gaming the numbers.
details: MTTD depends on event time and detection time semantics
MTTR varies by definition and may hide complex cases
Recall requires an estimate of missed attacks from tests/hunts
workflow: Document metric definition and window
Sample verified alerts and missed test events
Explain trends with detection changes and staffing context
lessons.example: A reduction in alerts after connector failure is a monitoring incident, not a precision improvement.
evidence: Rule hit counts with reviewed dispositions
Data freshness and tested simulation coverage
pitfalls: Ranking teams by closure speed alone
Ignoring skipped incidents in metrics

lessons.title: Windows forensic artifacts: Prefetch, Amcache and Shimcache
lessons.summary: Know what host execution artifacts can suggest—and why their presence or absence rarely proves exact execution sequences.
details: Prefetch can indicate application runs but depends on policy/OS
Amcache provides executable metadata with interpretation caveats
Shimcache/AppCompatCache is not a standalone execution proof
workflow: Preserve forensic image or targeted artifacts properly
Correlate with EDR, event logs and file timestamps
State limitations explicitly in report
lessons.example: A hash appears in Amcache near incident date; compare with Sysmon process and file activity before concluding execution.
evidence: Artifact path, source image hash and tool version
Corroborating process evidence
pitfalls: Treating every Shimcache entry as executed
Editing mounted evidence during triage

lessons.title: Memory forensics: volatile evidence fundamentals
lessons.summary: Understand why running processes, network sockets, injected memory and volatile secrets require a planned acquisition and integrity chain.
details: Memory acquisition can change the system and expose sensitive data
Volatility differs from disk persistence
Timeline and tooling must record collection context
workflow: Determine necessity and legal authorization
Acquire with validated tool and hashed output
Examine process/network anomalies with correlation to disk and logs
lessons.example: A disk scanner finds nothing after a short-lived in-memory process; available memory capture may add context, not guarantee attribution.
evidence: Acquisition timestamp, host state and SHA-256
Process/VAD/socket indicators with confidence
pitfalls: Running volatile capture without planning impact
Exposing secrets in unsecured evidence

lessons.title: Kubernetes audit and workload drift
lessons.summary: Detect high-risk API access, secret reads and unexpected workload modifications while considering the noisy automation of controllers and deployments.
details: Kubernetes audit policies determine what verbs/resources are logged
Service accounts and workload identities need identity mapping
A new privileged pod or hostPath mount can increase risk
workflow: Review API verb, actor, namespace and source
Compare against deploy controller/change window
Correlate pod image, permissions and network egress
lessons.example: create pods with privileged=true by unknown service account warrants urgent validation; legitimate agents may require exceptional privileges.
evidence: Kubernetes audit verb/resource/response
Pod spec, admission logs and RBAC grants
pitfalls: Assuming kube-apiserver access alone means breach
Ignoring policy-controlled audit omissions

lessons.title: SaaS audit engineering and coverage
lessons.summary: Model tenant administration, mailbox activities, OAuth apps and collaboration sharing across variable audit licensing and retention.
details: Some audit events require specific licenses and ingestion
SaaS identities span user, guest and service principals
Data-access auditing may not be on by default
workflow: Identify high-value SaaS workflows and critical roles
Verify event retention and field mapping
Build and test privileged activity analytics
lessons.example: A new guest invited into sensitive workspace after suspicious admin sign-in is context; review resource permissions and audit trail.
evidence: Tenant audit events and identity actor ID
Sharing policy and application consent history
pitfalls: Assuming all SaaS data actions logged by default
Ignoring guest/service principal activity

lessons.title: Threat-informed defense prioritization
lessons.summary: Connect business crown jewels, realistic threats, exposure and test outcomes to engineering investments instead of chasing every IOC feed.
details: Threat intelligence is useful when applicable to your environment
Technique mapping can prioritize telemetry and controls
Purple-team validation discovers practical gaps
workflow: Rank assets and attacker paths
Select high-impact techniques and test them safely
Prioritize durable telemetry and detection improvements
lessons.example: For a healthcare app, credential misuse and cloud-storage exports may be higher-priority hunt themes than malware family name feeds.
evidence: Threat model and asset owners
Emulation validation and remediation backlog
pitfalls: Equating feed count with coverage
Adopting framework mapping without business context

interviews.question: What is the SOC's primary purpose?
interviews.answer: Continuously detect, investigate and coordinate response to threats, using evidence from telemetry and business context.
interviews.trap: Saying the goal is to block every attack ignores incident coordination and risk.

interviews.question: Explain confidentiality, integrity and availability.
interviews.answer: Confidentiality restricts disclosure; integrity protects correctness; availability keeps services accessible. Give an example for each.
interviews.trap: Treating availability as only backup quality.

interviews.question: What is the difference between vulnerability, exploit and threat?
interviews.answer: A vulnerability is a weakness, an exploit is a way to abuse it, and a threat is a potential cause of harm.
interviews.trap: Confusing a CVE finding with confirmed exploitation.

interviews.question: What are indicators of compromise versus TTPs?
interviews.answer: IOCs are observable artifacts such as hashes/domains; TTPs describe adversary behaviors and procedures. Use both, but behavior often generalizes better.
interviews.trap: Assuming an IP hit proves malicious intent.

interviews.question: How do you explain a SIEM?
interviews.answer: It collects and normalizes log data, supports searching and correlation, and produces detections, dashboards and investigation context.
interviews.trap: Assuming SIEM automatically blocks attacks.

interviews.question: What is EDR versus antivirus?
interviews.answer: Traditional antivirus often emphasizes file/signature detection; EDR provides richer process telemetry, behavioral detection, investigation and response capabilities. Vendors overlap.
interviews.trap: Claiming antivirus never detects behavior.

interviews.question: What is MITRE ATT&CK?
interviews.answer: An evolving knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques based on observations, useful for organizing investigations and detection coverage.
interviews.trap: Calling it an incident response lifecycle.

interviews.question: Walk me through a DNS lookup.
interviews.answer: Client asks resolver; cache may answer; otherwise recursive resolution reaches authoritative name servers, returns record with TTL and client connects as appropriate.
interviews.trap: Saying DNS always uses UDP only.

interviews.question: TCP versus UDP?
interviews.answer: TCP is connection-oriented with reliability and ordering; UDP is datagram-based without those inherent guarantees. Apps can add controls, and QUIC uses UDP.
interviews.trap: Claiming UDP cannot be secure.

interviews.question: What happens in a TCP three-way handshake?
interviews.answer: SYN, SYN/ACK, ACK establish negotiated sequence state for TCP communication.
interviews.trap: Confusing ACK with the last step of teardown.

interviews.question: Name common ports useful to an analyst.
interviews.answer: 53 DNS, 80/443 web, 445 SMB, 3389 RDP, 22 SSH, 88 Kerberos, 389/636 LDAP, 25/587 SMTP. Verify actual protocol.
interviews.trap: Judging activity solely on the port number.

interviews.question: What does a 403 mean compared with a 401?
interviews.answer: 401 means authentication is required or failed; 403 indicates the server understood the request but refuses authorization. Implementation varies.
interviews.trap: Claiming 403 always means WAF blocked an exploit.

interviews.question: How does NAT complicate attribution?
interviews.answer: Many internal clients may share one public IP; need timestamp, source port, NAT translation and other logs.
interviews.trap: Treating external IP as an individual endpoint.

interviews.question: What is a proxy and why do analysts care?
interviews.answer: A proxy intermediates requests and can log destination URL, method, user, bytes and policy decisions with visibility dependent on deployment.
interviews.trap: Assuming encrypted body is always visible.

interviews.question: What is Event ID 4624?
interviews.answer: A successful Windows logon; logon type, account, source and context determine meaning.
interviews.trap: Calling every 4624 an interactive local login.

interviews.question: What is Event ID 4625?
interviews.answer: A failed Windows logon; aggregate counts, user/source distribution and nearby successful logons.
interviews.trap: Treating any single failure as brute force.

interviews.question: What is Event ID 4688?
interviews.answer: Process creation in Windows Security logs when relevant auditing is enabled; enhanced command line needs proper policy.
interviews.trap: Assuming command lines are always included.

interviews.question: What do Sysmon Events 1, 3 and 22 indicate?
interviews.answer: When configured: process creation, network connection and DNS query respectively.
interviews.trap: Assuming all Sysmon configurations collect all three.

interviews.question: What is an unusual process chain?
interviews.answer: A parent-child process relationship inconsistent with normal workflow, e.g., a document app spawning script interpreter with network egress. Needs context.
interviews.trap: Calling powershell.exe inherently malicious.

interviews.question: Where would you investigate SSH failures?
interviews.answer: Use auth journal/log files appropriate to distro, sshd service events and source/user aggregation. Check logging configuration.
interviews.trap: Assuming /var/log/auth.log exists everywhere.

interviews.question: How do you check listening services?
interviews.answer: Use ss -tulpn with appropriate privileges; correlate services with process owner and known change requests.
interviews.trap: Assuming any unfamiliar open port is malicious.

interviews.question: What are the first steps after a critical alert?
interviews.answer: Validate signal and timestamp, identify asset/user, assess active impact, consult playbook, correlate evidence and escalate urgently with clear findings.
interviews.trap: Isolating production assets without approval.

interviews.question: How do you decide severity?
interviews.answer: Consider impact, asset importance, affected identity privileges, scope, attacker activity, confidence and organizational severity matrix.
interviews.trap: Equating number of alerts to severity.

interviews.question: Difference between false positive and benign positive?
interviews.answer: False positive reflects detector mismatch; benign positive accurately identifies matching but authorized/harmless behavior. Labels vary across teams.
interviews.trap: Calling all approved scanner alerts false positives.

interviews.question: What belongs in an escalation ticket?
interviews.answer: Who, what, when (timezone), affected assets/accounts, evidence, investigation steps, confidence, business impact and requested actions.
interviews.trap: Writing 'suspicious, please check' without pivots.

interviews.question: How do you handle a noisy alert?
interviews.answer: Validate representative hits, use business context, identify tuning candidate, then follow change/review process rather than blindly suppressing it.
interviews.trap: Disabling a rule due only to alert count.

interviews.question: What should a shift handover include?
interviews.answer: Outstanding high-priority cases, status, owners, blockers, next actions, connector gaps and deadlines.
interviews.trap: Only reporting closed ticket counts.

interviews.question: What is password spraying?
interviews.answer: Low-volume attempts against many users, often to avoid account lockout; compare distinct users, source distribution and any success.
interviews.trap: Calling all multiple failures brute force.

interviews.question: What is an impossible-travel alert?
interviews.answer: Sign-ins from geographically distant locations in an unlikely time; verify VPN, shared exits, device/session and token activity.
interviews.trap: Treating IP geolocation as exact.

interviews.question: What are MFA fatigue signs?
interviews.answer: Repeated unexpected push prompts, denial then acceptance, changes to MFA methods and suspicious session context.
interviews.trap: Assuming MFA success is proof of legitimate user.

interviews.question: What is Kerberos used for?
interviews.answer: Ticket-based authentication in domain environments; TGT and service tickets support authenticated access without sending passwords to every service.
interviews.trap: Saying Kerberos encrypts all subsequent SMB file traffic automatically.

interviews.question: How do SPF, DKIM and DMARC differ?
interviews.answer: SPF validates authorized sender infrastructure, DKIM signs messages, DMARC aligns authenticated identifiers and states domain policy.
interviews.trap: Assuming passing SPF proves a message is safe.

interviews.question: How do you triage a reported phishing email?
interviews.answer: Collect headers and URLs safely, check sender auth and brand impersonation, search recipients, confirm user interaction, correlate sign-ins and recommend response.
interviews.trap: Clicking a suspicious URL on your main workstation.

interviews.question: What indicators distinguish BEC from ordinary spam?
interviews.answer: Contextual account compromise, payment diversion, unusual mailbox rules, impersonation and changes to established business process.
interviews.trap: Relying only on a suspicious attachment.

interviews.question: What is SQL injection in interview terms?
interviews.answer: Untrusted input changes the structure or semantics of a database query; parameterized queries reduce risk. Log requests alone do not prove execution.
interviews.trap: Claiming a WAF alert confirms database exfiltration.

interviews.question: What is XSS?
interviews.answer: Untrusted content is executed in another user's browser due to unsafe output handling; relevant kinds include reflected, stored and DOM-based.
interviews.trap: Confusing it with server-side code execution.

interviews.question: What is SSRF?
interviews.answer: An application can be tricked into making unintended server-side requests, potentially reaching internal or cloud metadata resources.
interviews.trap: Assuming SSRF always grants RCE.

interviews.question: Show a basic Splunk failed-login query.
interviews.answer: index=windows EventCode=4625 | stats count by src_ip, user | sort - count; adjust to actual sourcetype and fields.
interviews.trap: Pretending field names are universal.

interviews.question: Explain KQL summarize.
interviews.answer: It groups rows and computes aggregates such as count() by UserPrincipalName, optionally after a where time filter.
interviews.trap: Equating summarize with rendering a chart.

interviews.question: What is an alert's data source versus detection logic?
interviews.answer: Source is the telemetry generating events; detection logic is the condition/aggregation identifying matches. Both must be validated.
interviews.trap: Blaming the rule when source logs are missing.

interviews.question: How do you form a hypothesis?
interviews.answer: Write a falsifiable claim explaining evidence, identify alternatives, then find independent telemetry to support or reject each.
interviews.trap: Cherry-picking only confirming data.

interviews.question: How do you reconstruct an attack timeline?
interviews.answer: Normalize to UTC, join reliable identifiers and capture source/evidence for initial access, execution, persistence, lateral movement and impact.
interviews.trap: Assuming ingest time equals event time.

interviews.question: How would you investigate suspected account takeover?
interviews.answer: Review sign-ins and device/MFA context, investigate session and OAuth activity, assess accessed resources and mailbox rules, coordinate authorized revocation.
interviews.trap: Resetting password and assuming stolen sessions are gone.

interviews.question: How would you scope ransomware?
interviews.answer: Confirm malicious process/files, find host set and spread path, check privileged access and backups, preserve evidence, coordinate rapid authorized containment.
interviews.trap: Rebooting all endpoints before collecting evidence.

interviews.question: How can you detect lateral movement?
interviews.answer: Correlate remote logons, network SMB/WinRM/RDP, remote service/task creation, privileged account use and endpoint process trees.
interviews.trap: Calling every SMB connection lateral movement.

interviews.question: How do you evaluate DNS tunneling?
interviews.answer: Look at long/high-entropy subdomains, TXT activity, periodicity, volume and process/network correlation; test normal explanations.
interviews.trap: Labeling any long DNS name malicious.

interviews.question: What does a 200 HTTP response prove?
interviews.answer: It proves the server returned a successful status, not that an injection succeeded or sensitive data was stolen. Need app and backend evidence.
interviews.trap: Concluding compromise from 200 alone.

interviews.question: How do you assess cloud key abuse?
interviews.answer: Identify key/principal, API actions, origin, resource, privilege, time and deviations; correlate IaC changes and data access.
interviews.trap: Assuming all admin API calls are hostile.

interviews.question: Difference between containment, eradication and recovery?
interviews.answer: Containment limits threat, eradication removes malicious cause/persistence, recovery restores services with verification and monitoring.
interviews.trap: Treating isolation as eradication.

interviews.question: What is chain of custody?
interviews.answer: Documented handling and transfers showing artifact origin, integrity, dates, persons and storage; often supported by hashing.
interviews.trap: Using hashes as a substitute for access logs.

interviews.question: How do you decide whether to isolate a host?
interviews.answer: Consider active threat, asset criticality, connectivity, evidence, business continuity, containment alternatives and policy/approval.
interviews.trap: Always isolating a domain controller automatically.

interviews.question: How do you communicate to incident leadership?
interviews.answer: State verified facts, impact, confidence, decisions needed, action owners and next update; avoid unsupported attribution.
interviews.trap: Confusing guesses with observed data.

interviews.question: Explain precision versus recall.
interviews.answer: Precision is TP/(TP+FP); recall is TP/(TP+FN). Tuning must weigh analyst load against missed detections.
interviews.trap: Claiming fewer alerts always means better detection.

interviews.question: How would you tune a noisy detection?
interviews.answer: Analyze examples, form narrow exclusions, test historical malicious cases, use change control and monitor outcomes.
interviews.trap: Whitelisting entire organizational networks.

interviews.question: What is Sigma?
interviews.answer: A generic YAML detection rule format describing log source and match conditions; backends need accurate field mappings to work.
interviews.trap: Assuming Sigma YAML runs directly in every SIEM.

interviews.question: What is threat hunting versus triage?
interviews.answer: Triage responds to detections; hunting proactively tests behavior hypotheses across telemetry, documents negative results and proposes detection improvements.
interviews.trap: Treating IOC search as the only form of hunting.

interviews.question: What makes a useful hunting hypothesis?
interviews.answer: Threat behavior, affected scope, required observable events, falsification criteria and timeframe, grounded in intelligence or local risk.
interviews.trap: Searching first and making a hypothesis after seeing results.

interviews.question: How do you measure coverage?
interviews.answer: Map critical behaviors to prevention, log collection and validated detection, then test with approved emulation and measure outcome.
interviews.trap: Claiming ATT&CK IDs on rules prove coverage.

interviews.question: Describe detection-as-code.
interviews.answer: Detections live in version control with metadata, reviews, tests and deploy/rollback processes; deployment is observable.
interviews.trap: Skipping realistic negative test cases.

interviews.question: What does a strong detection specification include?
interviews.answer: Behavior hypothesis, sources/fields, logic, known benign cases, threshold, tests, ATT&CK reference, triage guide and owner.
interviews.trap: Starting with only a regex.

interviews.question: How do you validate a new rule?
interviews.answer: Run on positive and negative examples, historical log windows, check data sources and review performance and false-positive rate before production.
interviews.trap: Assuming one successful test covers variants.

interviews.question: What is a detection coverage gap?
interviews.answer: Required adversary behavior lacks prevention, reliable telemetry or validated alerting for relevant assets and circumstances.
interviews.trap: Confusing no alerts with good coverage.

interviews.question: Why preserve volatile evidence?
interviews.answer: Memory, processes and network state may disappear with shutdown/reboot; collect safely with legal and business approval.
interviews.trap: Assuming every host should be live-imaged regardless of impact.

interviews.question: Why is hash matching insufficient for malware hunting?
interviews.answer: Minor binary changes alter hashes; behavior, relationships and semantic features can detect related variants.
interviews.trap: Assuming a negative hash search means clean.

interviews.question: What signs suggest Kubernetes credential abuse?
interviews.answer: Unexpected service-account-token use, abnormal API calls, role bindings, pod execution or secrets access, correlated with workloads and deployment changes.
interviews.trap: Claiming any kubectl exec is hostile.

interviews.question: How do you conduct a blameless PIR?
interviews.answer: Reconstruct verified timeline, identify contributing control/process failures, assign measurable fixes and verify outcomes without personal blame.
interviews.trap: Ending with only more user awareness training.

interviews.question: Which SOC metrics matter?
interviews.answer: Well-defined detection/response times, backlog age, escalation quality, alert precision, coverage and ingest health, segmented by severity.
interviews.trap: Maximizing closed alerts as the main KPI.

interviews.question: Walk me through opening a website from the URL to first page load.
interviews.answer: DNS/cache lookup, TCP or QUIC connectivity, TLS and HTTP exchange, then browser rendering. In SOC, different logs record distinct stages; state what each actually proves.
interviews.trap: Jumping straight to HTTP without DNS/network context.

interviews.question: Differentiate Windows events 4624, 4625 and 7045.
interviews.answer: 4624 is successful logon; 4625 failed logon in Security; 7045 is service installation in System. They answer different questions and need source context.
interviews.trap: Claiming 7045 is a Security event or that type 3 is RDP.

interviews.question: What is the difference between Sysmon Event 1 and Event 3?
interviews.answer: Configured Sysmon Event 1 is process creation with rich process context; Event 3 represents network connections when enabled. Combine them via ProcessGuid and time.
interviews.trap: Assuming Event 3 is enabled everywhere.

interviews.question: How do you investigate a logon event outside business hours?
interviews.answer: Check account, logon type, source host/IP, device, MFA, change window and behavior after the session; compare user baseline and asset criticality.
interviews.trap: Calling every off-hours logon malicious.

interviews.question: Why can an impossible-travel alert be benign?
interviews.answer: VPN egress, corporate proxies, mobile network geolocation and cached sessions distort physical location. Validate ASN, egress, device and sequence.
interviews.trap: Saying geo alone proves an attacker.

interviews.question: What checks do you perform if a SIEM dashboard suddenly has zero alerts?
interviews.answer: Inspect ingestion delay, connector heartbeats, source event volume, parser changes, rule state and timeframe before inferring lower threat activity.
interviews.trap: Celebrating zero alerts without data health checks.

interviews.question: Does SPF/DKIM/DMARC pass make a message trustworthy?
interviews.answer: No. They test parts of sender authentication/alignment, not the sender intent; a compromised legitimate account can send convincing harmful content.
interviews.trap: Equating valid email authentication with no phishing risk.

interviews.question: How do you distinguish delivered, clicked, downloaded and executed?
interviews.answer: Mail gateway confirms receipt, proxy/browser click, web download, and EDR/process telemetry execution. Report each stage independently.
interviews.trap: Calling infection confirmed based on URL click alone.

interviews.question: What does an alert-only EDR action mean?
interviews.answer: The system detected behavior, but it did not report prevention. Verify process execution, child activity, network traffic and available response actions.
interviews.trap: Saying the binary was quarantined when action=alert_only.

interviews.question: How do you hand over a P1 case to the next shift?
interviews.answer: Provide asset/account, incident summary, confirmed UTC timeline, current containment status, evidence references, pending decisions, contacts, next owner and deadline.
interviews.trap: Only sending the incident ticket number.

interviews.question: Explain severity vs priority with an example.
interviews.answer: Severity describes technical/business seriousness; priority also reflects urgency, exposure, exploit state, criticality and response SLA. A service account takeover on production is urgent.
interviews.trap: Treating CVSS or alert severity as the entire triage decision.

interviews.question: What indicators support password spraying?
interviews.answer: One/few origins attempt authentication across many accounts with low per-account attempts; correlate lockouts, later successes, device posture and privileged changes.
interviews.trap: Saying each account must have hundreds of failures.

interviews.question: What can you conclude from a WAF 403?
interviews.answer: The matching request was blocked if the rule/action is authoritative; inspect app logs and other request IDs before claiming failed or successful broader exploitation.
interviews.trap: Saying every request from that IP is blocked.

interviews.question: Give a 30-second escalation for suspected mailbox compromise.
interviews.answer: A finance mailbox sign-in from an unmanaged source was followed by a new external forwarding rule at 08:12 UTC. Scope and exfiltration are being validated; request approved identity containment and mailbox audit review.
interviews.trap: Claiming confirmed data loss before evaluating access.

interviews.question: Explain how you would investigate 4624 type 3 followed by 7045.
interviews.answer: Map source account/IP and LogonId to host and service creation time, inspect executable and process tree, validate change records, then hunt same account on other hosts.
interviews.trap: Assuming remote service execution is confirmed malicious without business context.

interviews.question: How do you investigate suspected Kerberoasting?
interviews.answer: Review 4769 request patterns, unusual source, SPNs, sensitive service accounts, encryption context and resulting authentication activity; do not infer password cracking from tickets alone.
interviews.trap: Calling all RC4 tickets malicious or claiming a cracked password.

interviews.question: What evidence suggests DCSync-like behavior?
interviews.answer: Suspicious directory replication operations and privileges from non-DC principals, corroborated with security auditing and account/host provenance, may justify escalation.
interviews.trap: Claiming one 4662 event is conclusive.

interviews.question: How do you make an incident timeline across systems?
interviews.answer: Normalize UTC and event/ingest times, reconcile drift, preserve raw artifact reference, state confirmed facts and ordering uncertainty, and separate hypothesis from observation.
interviews.trap: Sorting local clocks as if they were UTC.

interviews.question: What containment options exist for compromised identity?
interviews.answer: Session/token revocation, password/key rotation, disabling identity, reducing permissions and removing app grants are options coordinated with owner and incident command.
interviews.trap: Only resetting password when malicious app credentials remain active.

interviews.question: When would you isolate a host?
interviews.answer: Where ongoing execution or lateral movement risk outweighs operational impact, within approved incident runbook; preserve evidence and ensure remote response access/rollback.
interviews.trap: Isolating a critical production server without authorization.

interviews.question: What is the difference between management and data access events?
interviews.answer: Management events record resource/configuration actions; data events record object or resource operations where enabled. Investigate both to establish rights and actual access.
interviews.trap: Claiming CreateAccessKey alone proves data exfiltration.

interviews.question: How do you investigate consent phishing?
interviews.answer: Trace app registration/grant, delegated scopes, identity sessions, app API calls, accessed resources, app publisher and response/revocation requirements.
interviews.trap: Concluding password reset removes OAuth grants.

interviews.question: What should be done if an external principal can read cloud storage?
interviews.answer: Verify policy and access period, correlate object-read logs if available, seek approved permission revocation, preserve trail and assess sensitive data exposure.
interviews.trap: Confusing permission to read with confirmed download of all objects.

interviews.question: What evidence distinguishes ransomware precursor and active impact?
interviews.answer: Backup tampering and suspicious tooling are possible precursors; high-volume file encryption/renaming plus ransom notes strongly indicate active impact.
interviews.trap: Waiting for family attribution to respond to encryption.

interviews.question: How do you tune a noisy detection?
interviews.answer: Review representative alerts, identify stable benign context, write narrow versioned exceptions, replay positive and negative cases, measure operational effect and set an owner/expiry.
interviews.trap: Whitelisting all activity from a high-volume subnet.

interviews.question: Explain why regular DNS requests are not enough to prove C2.
interviews.answer: Many legitimate services poll periodically. Compare domain novelty, query shape, process owner, timing, bytes and known scheduled services.
interviews.trap: Calling beaconing based solely on uniform interval.

interviews.question: What is chain of custody?
interviews.answer: A documented record of who collected, accessed, transferred and stored an artifact, alongside timestamps, hashes, method and integrity controls.
interviews.trap: Assuming a hash alone proves custody.

interviews.question: How would you brief leadership while facts are changing?
interviews.answer: Use verified facts, affected business functions, confidence, current containment, unknowns, decisions needed and next update deadline; avoid premature breach declarations.
interviews.trap: Mixing assumptions into confirmed impact.

interviews.question: How do you start a hypothesis-driven hunt?
interviews.answer: Define adversary behavior, target asset group, timeframe, available data and falsifiable criteria; baseline cohorts, pivot across sources and capture findings and coverage gaps.
interviews.trap: Starting from arbitrary suspicious strings without a defined question.

interviews.question: Describe your detection-as-code release pipeline.
interviews.answer: Version controlled rule with schema prerequisites, positive/negative tests, peer review, staging, performance checks, controlled rollout, monitoring and rollback.
interviews.trap: Deploying from a copied blog query without validation.

interviews.question: What are precision and recall in SOC rules?
interviews.answer: Precision is true positives among alerts; recall is detected true positives among all actual positive cases, which requires realistic tested ground truth. Both are difficult to measure perfectly.
interviews.trap: Claiming a rule has 100% recall from the matches it already generated.

interviews.question: What would you investigate if a known-positive test stops alerting?
interviews.answer: Check event generation, collection health, parsing/schema changes, lookup enrichment, rule enablement, filtering and time window in that order; add regression coverage.
interviews.trap: Lowering severity before proving which stage failed.

interviews.question: Does mapping 100 rules to ATT&CK mean 100% coverage?
interviews.answer: No. Technique counts obscure telemetry availability, asset deployment, rule fidelity and validated outcomes. Use threat-relevant tests and monitored population.
interviews.trap: Presenting a heatmap as a control effectiveness guarantee.

interviews.question: What are limits of Shimcache and Amcache?
interviews.answer: These artifacts provide execution-related context and metadata with OS/version-dependent caveats; correlate with Prefetch, logs and EDR before asserting execution.
interviews.trap: Treating every artifact entry as indisputable executed malware.

interviews.question: How would you detect Kubernetes secret misuse?
interviews.answer: Review API verb/resource/principal/namespace, RBAC grants, new service accounts, controller baselines, pod identity and data access; verify audit policy coverage.
interviews.trap: Alerting on every secret read without baseline.

interviews.question: How can MTTR improve for the wrong reason?
interviews.answer: Prematurely closed tickets, excluding hard cases, instrumentation outages and changed measurement definitions can all improve the number without improving security.
interviews.trap: Optimizing closures rather than validated response quality.

interviews.question: How do you prioritize engineering work across threats?
interviews.answer: Combine business crown jewels, credible attacker paths, existing coverage, detection test results and remediation cost; record owner and validation metrics.
interviews.trap: Chasing every new threat feed equally.

interviews.question: What should a good post-incident review produce?
interviews.answer: Timeline, root/compounding factors, what worked, telemetry gaps, actionable prioritized fixes with owners, due dates and verification tests, without blame.
interviews.trap: Writing a narrative but tracking no corrective actions.
